title: Measuring the Inflammation You Cannot See

patient.name: Mr Benjamin Oh Wei Liang
patient.presenting_complaint: Follow-up visit — known anterior uveitis right eye, on treatment, for flare measurement to monitor inflammation

history.hpc: Mr Oh was diagnosed with acute anterior uveitis in his right eye 3 weeks ago, presenting with redness, pain, and photophobia. He was started on intensive topical steroid drops with a tapering schedule. He reports his symptoms have improved significantly — pain and photophobia have largely resolved, though he notices mild residual blurring. He has been referred for a flare eye test to objectively measure the level of inflammation remaining in the anterior chamber before the doctor decides on tapering the steroid further.
history.pmhx: Anterior uveitis right eye, first episode, diagnosed 3 weeks ago. No known systemic autoimmune disease (currently being investigated). No previous eye surgery.
medications: Prednisolone acetate 1% eye drops right eye, currently 4 times daily on taper
Cyclopentolate 1% eye drops right eye OD
history.social_hx: Software engineer. Non-smoker. No known drug allergies.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right eye: mild residual conjunctival injection, few fine keratic precipitates on corneal endothelium, pupil sluggish from cycloplegic. Left eye: normal.
examination_findings.fundus: Not assessed today — anterior segment focus

flare_test_right.method: Laser flare meter, non-contact, patient fixates on internal target while a low-power laser beam is passed through the anterior chamber
flare_test_right.result: Significant reduction in flare compared to diagnosis, but still above normal range — indicates residual but improving anterior chamber inflammation

flare_test_left.result: Normal — no significant inflammation in left eye

investigations.iop_note: Right eye IOP 17 mmHg, mildly elevated compared to left — to monitor for steroid-induced IOP rise given prolonged topical steroid use

diagnosis: Flare eye test performed on both eyes using laser flare meter. Right eye flare value has decreased substantially from 45.2 to 18.5 photon counts/ms, indicating improving but still active anterior chamber inflammation. Left eye normal. For doctor's review regarding steroid tapering schedule and IOP monitoring.

immediate: Confirm patient identity and confirm both eyes are to be tested for comparison
Explain the procedure: a low-power laser beam (not visible/harmful) is passed through the front of the eye to measure protein levels, painless, non-contact
Set up the laser flare meter and enter patient details accurately
Position patient at chinrest with forehead against the rest in a darkened room for accurate measurement
Ask patient to fixate on the internal fixation target and keep the eye still during measurement
Take repeated measurements for the right (affected) eye and the left (unaffected) eye for comparison, recording the flare value in photon counts/ms for each
Retrieve the flare value from the diagnosis visit 3 weeks ago for comparison
Document IOP findings alongside flare results, given the patient is on intensive topical steroids
Print/document the report and hand to doctor, highlighting both the flare trend and the IOP value
follow_up: Doctor to review flare trend and decide on steroid tapering schedule
Doctor to review IOP given mild elevation on prolonged steroid use — may need to monitor for steroid response
Repeat flare test at next follow-up to continue tracking resolution of inflammation
patient_education: Explain that the flare value measures inflammation that may not be visible just by looking at the eye, helping guide how quickly to taper his steroid drops
Reinforce the importance of not stopping steroid drops abruptly, as this can cause rebound inflammation — follow the doctor's tapering schedule
Advise patient to report any new eye pain, redness, or visual changes promptly, as uveitis can recur

key_points: Confirms patient identity and reviews the clinical context (known anterior uveitis on steroid taper)
Asks about current symptoms and compares with symptoms at diagnosis to gauge clinical improvement
Reviews current medication regimen, including steroid dose and tapering status
Explains the non-contact, painless nature of the flare test to the patient
Sets up the laser flare meter correctly in a darkened room and enters patient data accurately
Positions patient correctly and obtains stable fixation for accurate measurement
Tests both the affected and unaffected eye for comparison and takes repeated measurements
Documents flare values in correct units (photon counts/ms) and retrieves prior values for trend comparison
Recognises that a decreasing flare value indicates improving anterior chamber inflammation
Identifies that the flare value remains above normal, indicating inflammation has not fully resolved
Notes the mildly elevated IOP in the right eye as a possible steroid response requiring monitoring
Does not adjust the steroid tapering schedule independently — refers trend data to doctor
Documents flare values and IOP for both eyes accurately, including trend comparison with prior visit
Hands report to doctor highlighting both the flare trend and the IOP finding
Educates patient on the importance of adherence to the steroid tapering schedule
Advises patient on symptoms of recurrence and when to seek urgent review
